positive: Place the learned institutional example in New France and its late-seventeenth/early-eighteenth-century setting. Explain the relationship between the French crown and appointed colonial officials, including the governor’s defence/diplomatic role and the intendant’s justice, administration and finance work; recognise that they also cooperated and had overlapping responsibilities.

Describe actual learned Catholic institutional roles, including religion and specific school/care examples. Identify a supported relationship such as the Ursulines’ education of girls or the Augustinians’ hospital work without assuming all people shared one belief, attended the same institution or had equal access.

Explain the studied seigneur/habitant landholding and responsibility relationship, using supported land, rent/labour or mill examples and why these mattered to settlers. Distinguish it from the colony’s governing offices rather than transplant a medieval king–knight–serf pyramid.

Use this knowledge to interpret a fresh attributed account of a settler-era administration, land or community-service situation, identifying a supported institution/role and explaining what remains uncertain. A colonial land grant or map does not by itself establish that Indigenous land was empty or that all Indigenous rights ended.
nearMiss: Uses modern elected Canadian Parliament/school boards or GovernorArthurPhillip as NewFrance’s institutions.
Calls every official the king or every habitant a knight-bound medieval serf.
Names Church or seigneur without explaining a supported role/importance; claims a European grant proved Indigenous land was empty or extinguished all rights.
claimCuration.transfer: Use a fresh attributed settler-era account of a land, administration or community-service matter to identify the relevant studied institution and supported role, or explain what source fact is missing. Preserve the account’s time, place and colonial perspective.
claimCuration.consumerBoundary: New ID has no inherited learner mastery. No estimate transfer or learner-state mutation is part of curation.

facts: The French crown appointed colonial officials. After the 1663 reorganisation, the governor retained major military and diplomatic responsibilities; the intendant oversaw justice, internal administration and finance.
The officials also cooperated, including on reports, land grants and trade matters; their responsibilities were not perfectly separate boxes.
royal-administration.limits: This describes a colonial administration’s institutions and ambitions, not a modern verdict on Indigenous sovereignty/title or an endorsement of royal authority.

land-and-mill.period: New France, with a specific 1709 near-Québec map and seventeenth-century Richelieu-area explanation
facts: Seigneurs granted farm holdings to habitants within the colonial landholding system; both had specified responsibilities. The studied account describes a seigneur’s mill duty and habitant payments and work obligations.

The authentic 1709 map shows long plots around the St. Lawrence and Île d’Orléans; the object record explains water access. A colonial plot map records a particular landholding view, not every people’s territory or ownership.
land-and-mill.limits: No exact fee calculation, uniform plot-shape rule, all-habitants serfdom or Indigenous-rights conclusion. Source images remain attributed references, not copied into the public taxonomy.

school-and-care.period: Institutions established in 1639 and operating in the studied later-seventeenth-century setting; Hôpital général transfer in 1693
facts: The actual 19 September 1667 marriage record of Catherine Moitié and Désiré Viger at Notre-Dame de Montréal identifies the priest G. Perot and published marriage banns. The museum explains that parish priests announced banns at Mass. This is a concrete religious/community function for the studied Catholic settlers, distinct from teaching or hospital care; it does not establish every resident’s belief or experience.

The Ursulines arrived at Québec in 1639 and operated a school for girls; the source distinguishes early Indigenous pupils and later French-background pupils. Do not backdate its nineteenth-century curriculum or say every girl attended.

Augustinian sisters founded the Hôtel-Dieu in 1639 and were entrusted with the Hôpital général site in 1693 for care of older, sick, poor and wounded people. This is an institutional service role, not proof every patient recovered or every resident had equal access.
school-and-care.limits: Historical religious aims and services are described; learners need not adopt beliefs or take part in religious practice. Founding dates and later buildings are not interchangeable. The actual religious rite and register record are described, not prescribed to the learner.

facts: The governor’s concern is colonial defence.
The intendant’s concern is the administration/budget constraint. The source supports overlapping work rather than a guaranteed single official always winning.
changed-administration.originalScenario: Original fictional 1680s Québec case: the governor wants additional fortification work after receiving a military warning. The intendant reports that the requested spending exceeds the money allocated for the work. They need to consider the response and report to the crown. Why might both officials be involved, how do their learned roles explain their different concerns, and what further security/funding information would be needed before deciding what should happen? This is an authored example of the source-supported overlap, not a transcript of an actual dated dispute.
changed-administration.limits: No claim that this exact incident occurred, that one official had exclusive power over every spending decision or that a learner can determine a real legal outcome.
